# Sourcing interviews

Interviews are the highest-value evidence source the writing pipeline has, and the
discipline below keeps them ethical, reusable, and worth the interviewee's time.

Consent is layered and explicit: agreeing to talk is not agreeing to be quoted, and
agreeing to be quoted is not agreeing to be named. Each layer is confirmed
separately, in writing, before publication, and the interviewee sees their quotes in
final context before the piece ships. A quote whose owner hesitates is cut without
negotiation.

Preparation respects the hour: the interviewer arrives having read what the
interviewee has published, with questions their public work cannot answer. The first
minutes establish what the interviewee wants from the conversation, because an
interview that serves both sides produces the candid material a cold extraction
never reaches.

Recording happens only with explicit permission, and the transcript belongs to the
interview record with the same retention discipline as any working document. Details
shared off the record stay off the record even as background shading; if a detail
matters to a piece, the piece waits until the detail can be used properly.

Attribution defaults conservative: role-and-context attribution unless the
interviewee prefers their name, never the reverse. The relationship outlives the
piece — an interviewee who feels used is a source the whole function loses.

## Interview debt

Every published piece that leaned on an interview owes its interviewee two things
recorded at publication: the link, sent personally, and a note in the interview
record of what was used. The record keeps the relationship honest at re-contact
time — an interviewee asked again a year later deserves an interviewer who knows
exactly what their last hour produced.
